summary: A response to RFC 607's comments on the File Transfer Protocol. It is one of several notes on FTP changes, along with RFCs 624, 542 and 640.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC responds to a list of proposed changes to FTP. The authors agree with some suggestions, explain why they disagree with others, and propose several clarifications.

questions: what changes did rfc 614 suggest for ftp
subtitle: Answers to suggested changes for the early File Transfer Protocol.

tldr.problem: RFC 607 raised questions about FTP behavior, including passive transfers, handshaking, reply codes, and mail.
tldr.mechanism: Pogran and Neigus respond point by point, agreeing on some clarifications and arguing for other approaches to replies, transfer setup, and login behavior.
tldr.outcome: The authors propose changes such as fixed four-character commands, a minimum wait for a data connection, and requiring mail-sending programs to use MLFL.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 614 as Unknown and records that it updates RFCs 542 and 607. It is a response to discussion of an early FTP specification.

sections.title: Responding to RFC 607
sections.content:
Ken Pogran and N. Neigus answer comments on the File Transfer Protocol in RFC 607. They say they do not agree with every suggested change, but believe each issue deserves consideration.

The numbered paragraphs in RFC 614 correspond to the numbered comments in RFC 607.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors use the same numbering as the earlier comments. This makes it easier to match each response with the point being discussed.

sections.title: Passive Mode and Data Connections
sections.content:
The authors support a way to return a server to active mode and suggest replies that say whether its mode changed or was already active. They note that a server listening for a passive data connection may not see an ACTV command unless the user-FTP sends a Telnet SYNC sequence first.

They agree FTP commands should always have four characters. For a transfer, the user should listen on the data connection before sending the transfer command; the server checks the file before opening the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The note clarifies who should listen first and when the server checks a file. It also says commands should have a consistent length.

sections.title: Replies, Login, and Mail
sections.content:
The authors favor retaining the hyphen convention for multi-line replies and reject a simple rule that treats every 2xx reply as success. They call for a broader redesign of reply codes and propose merging two readiness replies into a clearer waiting response.

They agree that data after the final end-of-record marker should be discarded, propose removing the 331 reply for login requests, and recommend that mail-sending programs use MLFL rather than MAIL.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors prefer explicit reply handling and clearer login behavior. They also recommend a data connection for programs that send mail files.
